```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")
has_cograph <- requireNamespace("cograph", quietly = TRUE)
```

A questionnaire with many items can yield so many correlations that the most
informative relationships are difficult to see. Researchers studying motivation,
self-efficacy and self-regulation may want to examine these constructs together,
yet plotting every association creates a crowded network of variables connected
by edges. Selecting edges solely through a significance threshold can likewise
produce a dense graph that is difficult to interpret. Information-filtering
networks offer a structured means of retaining a manageable set of associations
while preserving a view of their interdependence. Filtering methods have been
studied in psychometric network research (Christensen et al., 2018). Exploratory
graph analysis also uses network structure, but for the distinct purpose of
investigating dimensionality (Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Golino et al., 2020).

Information-filtering networks extract a sparse, connected backbone from an
association matrix according to structural constraints rather than a
significance test or a regularisation penalty. The Triangulated Maximally
Filtered Graph (TMFG; Massara et al., 2016) constructs a planar graph from
strong correlations and retains exactly $3(p - 2)$ edges for $p$ variables.
The Local-Global method (LoGo; Barfuss et al., 2016) uses the cliques and
separators of this graph to estimate a sparse precision matrix and its partial
correlations, without selecting a penalty parameter. These methods therefore
provide two related descriptions of the data: TMFG edges express ordinary
pairwise correlations, whereas LoGo edges express conditional associations
within the fitted model after accounting for the other variables. Neither
kind of edge establishes a causal relationship.

Psychological networks have been used in educational research to investigate
relationships among learning processes and their development over time. For
example, Saqr et al. (2021) examined relational and temporal patterns of
self-regulation in academic writing, and Malmberg et al. (2022) used network
analysis to study associations between students' monitoring events and phases
of regulation. Saqr et al. (2024) discuss psychological network methods for
analysing learning and complex learning processes more broadly. These
applications illustrate why the pattern of connections among learning-related
variables can be of substantive interest. They also make it important to
distinguish a readable representation of associations from evidence about
causal mechanisms, stable network structure or individual learners.

This article demonstrates TMFG and LoGo using five self-regulated learning
construct scores supplied with the psychnets package. It first constructs a
correlation-based TMFG backbone and checks its structural properties, then
estimates LoGo partial correlations and examines their optimality, node
centralities and predictability. Finally, it visualises the network, repeats
the analysis using Spearman correlations and outlines reporting and
interpretation considerations. The responses were generated by a language
model rather than collected from students, so the example illustrates the
methods and their interpretation rather than empirical conclusions about
learners.

```{r setup}
library(psychnets)
```

## The model

TMFG begins with a set of four variables selected for their strong combined
correlations, forming a tetrahedron with six edges. Each remaining variable
is placed in the triangular face for which its connections to the three
vertices have the greatest combined weight. The new variable is connected
to those vertices, adding three edges. The construction therefore has

$$
6 + 3(p - 4) = 3(p - 2)
$$

edges, and the graph is connected, planar and chordal: it decomposes into
four-node cliques that overlap in three-node separators.

LoGo uses this decomposition to estimate the precision matrix. With
$\mathbf{S}$ the correlation matrix, $\mathcal{C}$ the four-node cliques and
$\mathcal{T}$ the three-node separators,

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{K}} = \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \left[\mathbf{S}_{cc}^{-1}\right]^{0}
- \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \left[\mathbf{S}_{tt}^{-1}\right]^{0},
$$

where $[\cdot]^0$ places a small inverse into the full $p \times p$ matrix with
zeros elsewhere. The result is the maximum-likelihood precision matrix of a
Gaussian model whose missing edges are exactly those absent from the TMFG, and
the partial correlations are
$\rho_{ij \cdot \mathrm{rest}} = -K_{ij}/\sqrt{K_{ii}K_{jj}}$.

## Data

`SRL_GPT` contains 300 sets of responses to items from the Motivated
Strategies for Learning Questionnaire, summarised as construct scores on a
scale from 1 to 7. The responses were generated by a large language model
(GPT) in a study of how such models answer psychological surveys
(Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). They provide a convenient worked example, but
should not be interpreted as observations of students or their learning.

- **Nodes:** five construct scores, treated as continuous: `CSU` (cognitive
  strategy use), `IV` (intrinsic value), `SE` (self-efficacy), `SR`
  (self-regulation) and `TA` (test anxiety).
- **Observations:** one row per respondent; the data are complete.

```{r data}
head(SRL_GPT)
```

With five nodes, a TMFG keeps $3(5 - 2) = 9$ of the 10 possible pairs, so the
example shows how the method works rather than how much it filters. Filtering
grows with the number of variables: with 30 items a TMFG keeps 84 of 435
pairs.

## Which correlations form the backbone?

`psychnet()` with `method = "tmfg"` builds the filtered graph from the Pearson
correlation matrix.

```{r tmfg}
tmfg_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "tmfg")
summary(tmfg_net)
as.data.frame(tmfg_net)
```

The backbone has 9 edges, with correlations from -0.302 to 0.861. The four
learning constructs are fully connected by strong positive correlations, from
0.779 (`SE`–`SR`) to 0.861 (`CSU`–`IV`). Test anxiety is attached through
three negative correlations, the strongest with self-regulation (-0.302). The
excluded pair is `SE`–`TA`. TMFG chooses edges as part of a connected
structure rather than by a cut-off, so an excluded pair is not necessarily
uncorrelated.

## Does the backbone have the required structure?

A TMFG is defined by its structure: exactly $3(p - 2)$ edges, connected,
planar and chordal. `certificate()` counts how many of these properties the
fitted graph violates.

```{r certificate-tmfg}
certificate(tmfg_net)
```

The count is 0 and `certified` is `TRUE`: the graph has all the properties
of a TMFG. This checks the construction, not the stability of the selected
edges across samples.

## Which associations remain after adjustment?

`psychnet()` with `method = "logo"` builds the same backbone and estimates
partial correlations on it.

```{r logo}
logo_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "logo")
summary(logo_net)
as.data.frame(logo_net)
```

The LoGo network has the same 9 edges, now carrying partial correlations. The
strongest positive edges join cognitive strategy use with intrinsic value
(0.404), self-efficacy (0.393) and self-regulation (0.377). Self-regulation and
test anxiety share the only negative edge (-0.372), slightly stronger than
their correlation of -0.302.

Comparing the two tables shows what adjustment does. The `IV`–`SE`
correlation is 0.785 but its partial correlation is 0.165. The association
between intrinsic value and self-efficacy is therefore considerably smaller
after adjustment for the other constructs. Test anxiety correlates negatively
with cognitive strategy use (-0.139) and intrinsic value (-0.114), whereas
its partial correlations with these constructs are positive (0.110 and 0.146).
These changes of sign reflect conditional associations in the fitted network;
they do not establish that self-regulation mediates the relationships. TMFG
and LoGo weights should therefore be reported and interpreted separately.

## Is the LoGo network the maximum-likelihood solution?

LoGo is a closed-form construction, and its result should be the
maximum-likelihood estimate for the TMFG graph. Any such solution must satisfy
the problem's optimality (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker) conditions: the implied
covariance reproduces the observed correlation on every retained edge and on
the diagonal, and the precision is zero on every missing edge. The amount by
which a fitted network violates them is its certificate; a value near zero
shows that the network is the optimum of its objective.

```{r certificate-logo}
certificate(logo_net)
```

The violation is at the level of machine precision (below $10^{-14}$), so the
LoGo partial correlations are the maximum-likelihood estimates for the
backbone.

## Which constructs are most connected?

`net_centralities()` returns strength, the sum of absolute edge weights, and
expected influence, the signed sum, for the LoGo network.

```{r centrality}
net_centralities(logo_net)
```

Cognitive strategy use has the largest strength (1.284), equal to its expected
influence because all its edges are positive. Self-regulation follows in
strength (1.247), but its negative edge with test anxiety lowers its expected
influence to 0.503. Test anxiety has the smallest strength (0.628) and a
negative expected influence (-0.116). Cognitive strategy use is the most
connected construct, and self-regulation is the link between the learning
constructs and test anxiety. Centrality describes the graph and does not
identify causes or intervention targets.

## How well is each construct predicted by the others?

`net_predict()` reports each node's $R^2$, computed from the LoGo precision
matrix as $R_j^2 = 1 - 1/(K_{jj}S_{jj})$.

```{r predictability}
net_predict(logo_net)
```

In the fitted Gaussian network, the other constructs account for
approximately 83% of the variance in cognitive strategy use
($R^2 = 0.835$), 79% in self-regulation, 78% in intrinsic value and 72% in
self-efficacy, but only 16% in test anxiety ($R^2 = 0.159$). The learning
constructs are largely predictable from one another, while test anxiety is
not. These are in-sample values.

## What does the network look like?

`cograph::splot()` draws the LoGo network, with green positive and red negative
edges and a ring showing each node's predictability.

```{r plot, eval = has_cograph}
cograph::splot(logo_net, psych_styling = TRUE, predictability = TRUE)
```

The figure shows the triangulated structure: four learning constructs fully
connected, and test anxiety attached to three of them. Node positions come
from a layout algorithm and carry no statistical meaning.

## Do the conclusions depend on the correlation estimator?

Refitting LoGo with `cor_method = "spearman"` bases both the backbone and the
partial correlations on rank correlations.

```{r spearman}
logo_spearman <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "logo",
                          cor_method = "spearman")
summary(logo_spearman)
as.data.frame(logo_spearman)
certificate(logo_spearman)
```

The rank-based backbone contains the same nine pairs. The positive edges of
cognitive strategy use remain the strongest, with `CSU`–`SE` (0.440) now
slightly above `CSU`–`IV` (0.412), and the `SR`–`TA` edge remains negative
(-0.301). The weak `CSU`–`TA` edge falls from 0.110 to 0.071. The certificate
is again at machine precision. For these data, the selected backbone and the principal associations
are similar under the two correlation estimators.

## Reporting the analysis

A report states the variables, the sample size, the correlation estimator and
the treatment of missing data, and keeps the two stages apart: TMFG edges are
correlations, LoGo edges are partial correlations.

In this analysis, TMFG on Pearson correlations of 300 complete responses kept
9 of 10 pairs, leaving out `SE`–`TA`. LoGo partial correlations on that
backbone were largest for cognitive strategy use with intrinsic value (0.404)
and negative only for self-regulation with test anxiety (-0.372). A rank-based
analysis kept the same backbone and the same main edges.

## Assumptions and when to use information filtering

- TMFG fixes the number of edges at $3(p - 2)$ whatever the sample size. It
  suits large item sets where a readable backbone is wanted and where a
  penalty-based method would keep too many or too few edges; it does not test
  whether an edge is different from zero.
- LoGo assumes a Gaussian model restricted to the TMFG graph. It needs no
  tuning parameter, but every four-node block of the correlation matrix must
  be invertible, so duplicated or perfectly collinear variables must be
  removed first.
- When the aim is to select conditional associations using a statistical
  selection criterion, graphical lasso or stepwise selection may be more
  appropriate. When the aim is to display a sparse set of marginal
  associations, the TMFG backbone can be examined on its own.
- Neither network identifies causal direction.
